title: Constant-round quantum refereed games versus \(\mathrm{PSPACE}\)
formal: Does \(\mathrm{QRG}_{\mathrm{const}}\subseteq\mathrm{PSPACE}\)? For every promise problem \(\Pi=(Y,N)\) admitting a quantum refereed game with a uniform polynomial-time verifier, two competing provers and some fixed constant \(k\) of interaction cycles, must there be a deterministic algorithm deciding \(\Pi\) using polynomial space? For \(x\in Y\), a yes-prover must have a strategy that makes the verifier accept with probability at least \(2/3\) against every no-prover strategy. For \(x\in N\), a no-prover must have a strategy that makes it reject with probability at least \(2/3\) against every yes-prover strategy. The constant \(k\) and the polynomial bounds may depend on the problem and verifier, but not on input length.
why: These games combine efficient quantum verification with competition between two powerful provers who have different information. Locating constant-length games would clarify whether repeated alternation of private interaction can increase computational power beyond polynomial space, even when only a few exchanges are allowed.
status_note: The July 2026 source asks the general constant-round question. The primary game definitions, polynomial-length EXP characterization and bounded-turn PSPACE results were checked on 2026-09-14, with a bounded later-work search. The one-switch/DQIP result does not settle arbitrary constant interleaving, and no full resolution was identified.

progress.text: Gutoski and Watrous establish the competing-prover model and short quantum games, emphasizing private messages and interaction order.
Gutoski and Watrous characterize polynomial-length quantum refereed games by EXP.
Gutoski and Wu prove DQIP = QRG(2) = PSPACE for their specified one-switch interaction pattern and leave more general bounded-turn games outside that characterization.
The source problem list reiterates the question for a general constant number of rounds.

sentences: A quantum refereed game has two competing provers trying to make an efficient verifier accept or reject.
The provers exchange private quantum messages with the verifier and may keep private memory.
The question asks whether every game with a constant number of interaction cycles can be simulated in deterministic polynomial space.
Polynomial-space simulations are known for specific patterns in which interaction switches from one prover to the other only once.
Polynomially many general rounds capture exponential time, leaving the full constant-round boundary open.

definitions:
A promise problem is a pair of disjoint sets \(Y,N\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\); no answer is prescribed outside their union. Both provers know the classical input \(x\) and the verifier's complete specification. The yes-prover seeks acceptance and the no-prover seeks rejection. They cannot communicate directly and do not initially share an entangled state or correlated private randomness. Each may retain private quantum memory throughout the interaction, use randomness, and perform arbitrary finite-dimensional quantum operations without a time or memory bound.

The verifier is generated from \(x\), of length \(n\), by one deterministic polynomial-time Turing machine. Its total gate count, workspace, and total communicated qubits are polynomial in \(n\). It starts with zero-initialized registers. In each of at most \(k\) cycles, it applies a quantum circuit, sends one message register privately to each prover, and receives both response registers. Each prover acts only on its current message and its own retained private memory. The verifier then proceeds to the next cycle or its final two-outcome measurement. Messages to the two provers may be entangled through the verifier's preparation; this is part of the specified protocol. Empty messages are allowed. Sequential exchanges can be scheduled in separate cycles, so allowing every fixed \(k\) includes any constant-length message pattern. The verifier never gives a prover access to the other prover's private channel unless its own prescribed operations deliberately convey information from it.

Use a fixed universal finite gate set: Hadamard maps \(|0\rangle\) to \((|0\rangle+|1\rangle)/\sqrt2\) and \(|1\rangle\) to \((|0\rangle-|1\rangle)/\sqrt2\); \(T\) multiplies \(|1\rangle\) by \(e^{i\pi/4}\) and fixes \(|0\rangle\); include \(T^{-1}\) and controlled NOT. The verifier's measurements, randomness and adaptive choices may be implemented coherently with polynomially many ancillary qubits. Prover operations are unrestricted quantum channels, expressible as \(\rho\mapsto\sum_j K_j\rho K_j^\dagger\) with \(\sum_j K_j^\dagger K_j=I\), on their message and private registers. Initial private states can be prepared by those channels. All winning probabilities are over the resulting quantum measurement outcomes and private randomization. Each winning strategy may depend on \(x\), but must work against every opposing strategy on that input.

The class \(\mathrm{PSPACE}\) consists here of promise problems decided by a deterministic multitape Turing machine with a read-only input tape and at most \(C(n+1)^r\) work-tape cells for fixed constants \(C,r\). It must halt on all inputs and give the correct answer on \(Y\cup N\). It has no oracle or advice. The simulator need only decide which side can force a win; it need not output either prover's strategy.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the inclusion, or of its negation. An inclusion proof must cover every fixed constant number of interaction cycles and every polynomial-time uniform verifier in the stated private-message model. A negative proof must exhibit a promise problem in this class with no deterministic polynomial-space decision algorithm. An exponential-time simulation, or a polynomial-space simulation only for one exchange pattern, does not suffice.

context_blocks.text: The winning-strategy requirements contain opposite quantifier orders on yes- and no-inputs. A prover must force its preferred outcome against all opposing strategies. This is different from two cooperating proof providers or a verifier receiving two unentangled existential witnesses.

Gutoski and Wu prove a polynomial-space simulation when all interaction with one prover is completed before interaction with the other begins. This includes their class QRG(2). Their result does not cover arbitrary repeated interleaving of the two private conversations.

Different papers count individual messages, turns and full send/receive rounds differently. This card fixes a complete interaction cycle explicitly. Since it asks about every constant cycle count, a constant change of counting convention does not change its scope.

With polynomially many messages, quantum refereed games capture \(\mathrm{EXP}\), deterministic time \(2^{\mathrm{poly}(n)}\). This gives an upper bound for constant-length games, but it does not supply a polynomial-space simulation. The constant-length question remains meaningful even for classical messages.
